second_opinion.reason: A real payment never requires you to pay a fee first. Asking you to send money to get money is a classic overpayment and advance-fee trick.
Scammers use a Google Voice code to set up an account in your name; never share a verification code with a stranger.
Real police never demand payment by prepaid card to cancel a warrant; this is a classic jury duty scam meant to scare you into paying.
Real utility companies never demand Bitcoin ATM payments or threaten to cut power within 45 minutes; this is a classic pressure scam.
This is a classic "wrong number" opener: a stranger pretends to have texted by mistake, then tries to start a friendly chat, often leading to investment or romance fraud.
A real bank never asks you to read out a texted code; scammers use it to break into your account.
Real landlords don't ask for a deposit through Cash App before you've even seen the apartment; this is a common rental scam.
This is a classic "Hi Dad, new number" trick where a scammer pretends to be your child and rushes you to send money to an unknown account.
A surprise cashback prize with a shortened link is a classic trick to steal your DANA login or money; DANA doesn't hand out prizes this way.
This is a fake renewal notice with a big charge meant to scare you into calling a number, where scammers then ask for your bank details or computer access.
No real investor can guarantee 30% daily returns. This is a classic investment lure that uses fake urgency to pull you into a private chat.
Real toll agencies don't text payment links from odd websites; this fake toll bill rushes you to pay a small fee and hand over card details.
This looks like a normal Uber login code, and it warns you not to share it. Just don't give it to anyone who asks.
This looks like a normal card alert. It asks you to call the number on your card, not click a link or share details.
Real Amazon delivery notices look like this, but scammers copy them too, so don't tap any link and check Your Orders in the Amazon app.
It's a casual family message with no request for money, links, or personal information, though it's worth confirming the sender is who they claim to be.
This is a routine appointment reminder with no links, payment requests, or personal information requested, just a simple reply to confirm or reschedule.
This looks like an ordinary school notice about a field trip, with a small fee paid in person at the school office, and it has no links or requests for personal information.
This is a normal interview scheduling note with no links, requests for money or personal details, or pressure, though it's wise to confirm through the company's official site.
This looks like a friend asking to split a concert ticket cost, with no links, urgency, or pressure, though confirm it's really them before paying.
It only mentions a bill amount and due date, with no link or urgent demand, and points to the official app or office.
The sender address "account.netflix.com" is not Netflix's real domain (netflix.com), so this could be a fake alert. Don't click anything; check your account in the official app.
This looks like a routine pharmacy pickup reminder with no links, payment requests, or personal information asked for, and "today" is just normal pickup timing.
This is a routine airline gate-change notice with no links, requests for money, or personal information.
This is a routine Google sign-in notice from Google's own address, and it asks you to click nothing and send nothing. No action is needed unless you don't recognize the sign-in.
This looks like a real USPS Informed Delivery digest, but it's a common phishing copycat, so don't tap links and check in the official USPS app.
This is a standard one-time code text that warns you never to share the code, and it asks you to do nothing.
